items.title: Focus Question: How does a thin layer of gasoline on a wet road produce a rainbow of colors?

body.html: A very thin layer of fuel floats on water. We want to explain the colored swirls.

Light reflects from the top surface of the fuel and from the fuel-water boundary underneath. These two reflected waves are coherent (same source) and interfere. Whether a given color is reinforced depends on the film thickness 𝑑, the index 𝑛 and the wavelength.

The fuel layer is not the same thickness everywhere. At each spot the extra path 2𝑑 matches the reinforcement condition for a different wavelength. White light holds every color, so each spot sends back whichever color is reinforced there, and the road shows swirls of many colors.

answer.html: The fuel layer is a thin film of varying thickness. Each color is reinforced where its wavelength meets the constructive condition, so different thicknesses look like different colors.

check.html: Where the layer is thicker than a few micrometers the colors wash out, because many wavelengths are reinforced at once and the sum looks white.

items.title: Figure 4 caption question: A student wants to demonstrate single-slit diffraction of green laser light (𝜆= 520 nm) with a slit 2.0 cm wide. Why will this slit not work, and what slit width would?

body.html: 𝜆= 5.20 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> m, 𝑤= 2.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m. Unknown: why the slit is a poor choice, and a better width.
A slit spreads light noticeably only when its width is within roughly tens to hundreds of wavelengths. It must also be wide enough to pass enough light.
Count wavelengths across the slit.

The slit is about 38,000 wavelengths wide, so the light barely bends and you would see a sharp-edged patch of light. A slit of tens to hundreds of wavelengths, that is about 5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> m to 5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> m (0.005 mm to 0.05 mm), would spread the light into a visible pattern.

answer.html: The 2.0 cm slit is about 3.8 × 10<sup>4</sup> wavelengths wide, so there is almost no spreading. A slit near 0.01 to 0.05 mm wide passes enough light and still diffracts it strongly.

check.html: A slit of 0.020 mm is 0.020 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> / 5.20 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> ≈38 wavelengths wide, inside the "tens of wavelengths" range.

items.title: Get It? (p. 451): Describe how the pattern of colors on a peacock feather forms.

body.html: Thin, layered structures reflect light from each interface.

answer.html: Light reflects from the top and bottom of microscopic layers in the feather barbules. The reflected waves are coherent, so for the wavelength where they arrive in phase they reinforce, and other colors are weakened. The reinforced color depends on layer thickness and the angle at which you look, so the feather appears to shimmer as it moves.

items.title: 10: Green laser light (𝜆= 520 nm) shines on two narrow slits. Describe how the light behaves at the slits and why the screen shows bright and dark regions. Sketch the pattern.

body.html: Diffraction and superposition.

Each narrow slit diffracts the green light into a nearly cylindrical wavefront (Huygens). The two wavefronts overlap beyond the barrier. At a point where the paths from the two slits differ by a whole number of wavelengths (0, 𝜆, 2𝜆, … ), crests arrive together and the spot is bright. Where they differ by a half wavelength plus a whole number, a crest meets a trough and the spot is dark. The screen shows a bright central band with evenly spaced bright and dark bands on both sides. See the upper strip in the sketch.

answer.html: Each slit spreads the light by diffraction. Where path lengths from the two slits differ by 𝑚𝜆 the waves reinforce (bright); where they differ by (𝑚+<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>)𝜆 they cancel (dark). The pattern is a bright central band with equally spaced bright and dark bands on both sides.

check.html: The central band is bright because both paths are equal (𝑚= 0).

items.title: Focus Question: How do bubbles produce a rainbow effect?

body.html: Light reflects from both surfaces of the soap film. The two reflected waves are coherent (same source) and interfere. For a film of thickness 𝑑 and index 𝑛, the condition for reinforcement depends on the wavelength in the film, so different colors are reinforced at different thicknesses.

The film thickness varies across the bubble (and changes as the liquid drains), and the light hits at different angles. At each spot a different wavelength meets the constructive condition, so each spot looks a different color. White light contains all colors, so the bubble shows a rainbow of bands.

answer.html: A bubble film is a thin film with varying thickness. Each color is reinforced at a different thickness, so the film shows a spectrum of colors.

check.html: Where the film is extremely thin (top of a vertical film) no visible color is reinforced, so it looks black, which is what you see just before a bubble pops.

items.title: Figure 4 caption question: why are the slit widths tens to hundreds of wavelengths?

body.html: A slit spreads (diffracts) light well only if its width is not much bigger than 𝜆, but it must be big enough to pass enough light.

If the slit were hundreds of thousands of wavelengths wide, there would be almost no spreading and you would just get a sharp shadow edge. If it were narrower than about one wavelength, almost no light would get through. Tens to hundreds of wavelengths gives a bright, usefully spread, nearly cylindrical wavefront.

answer.html: At that width the slit passes enough light and still diffracts it into nearly cylindrical wavefronts that overlap and interfere.

check.html: Visible light has 𝜆≈5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> m, so slits of about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> to 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> m (tens of micrometers up to 0.1 mm) fit.

items.title: Get It? (p. 451): How did the pattern on the hummingbird form?

answer.html: Light reflects from the top and bottom surfaces of thin layered structures in the feathers (thin-film interference). The two reflected waves are coherent. For the wavelength where they arrive in phase (including any inversion on reflection) they reinforce, so that color is bright, and other colors are dimmed. The reinforced color depends on thickness and viewing angle, so it shimmers.

items.title: 10 (Interference with two slits and red light)

question.html: Describe how a wave behaves at a slit and why some regions are bright and others dark. Sketch the pattern.

body.html: Diffraction and superposition.

Each narrow slit diffracts the red light, spreading it into a nearly cylindrical wavefront (Huygens). The two wavefronts overlap beyond the barrier. At a point where the path lengths from the two slits differ by a whole number of wavelengths (0, 𝜆, 2𝜆, … ), the crests arrive together, so the waves add and the spot is bright (constructive interference). Where the path lengths differ by a half wavelength plus a whole number, a crest meets a trough, the waves cancel, and the spot is dark (destructive interference). The result is a central bright band with evenly spaced bright and dark bands on both sides, dimmer farther out. See the sketch below.

answer.html: Each slit spreads the light by diffraction. Where path lengths from the two slits differ by 𝑚𝜆 the waves reinforce (bright); where they differ by (𝑚+<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>)𝜆 they cancel (dark). The pattern is a bright central band with equally spaced bright and dark bands on both sides.

check.html: The central band is bright because both paths are equal (𝑚= 0).

items.title: 14 (Critical thinking: small angle approximation)

question.html: How large can 𝜃 be before sin𝜃≈tan𝜃 fails with two significant figures? What happens when the precision increases?

body.html: tan𝜃/ sin𝜃= 1 / cos𝜃. The approximation is good while the relative difference is smaller than the rounding uncertainty of the data.
With two significant figures the uncertainty is about 1%. Relative difference = 1 / cos𝜃−1: 𝜃 sin𝜃
difference 3° 0.0523 0.0524 0.14% 𝜃 sin𝜃

difference 5° 0.0872 0.0875 0.38% 8° 0.1392 0.1405 0.98% 10° 0.1736 0.1763 1.5% A 1% difference occurs near 8°. With a stricter precision (three significant figures, about 0.1%), the difference is already 0.14% at 3°, so the limit drops to about 2.6°.

answer.html: About 5° to 8° (roughly 0.1 rad) for two significant figures. With greater precision the maximum valid angle decreases (about 2.6° for 0.1%).
